title: How backtracking explodes
summary: Watch the engine backtrack, spot the pattern shapes that take exponential time, and fix them: rewrite so each character matches one way, or use an atomic group.

steps.title: The engine tries every way before it says no
body: The .NET engine (like those in JavaScript, Python, Java and PCRE) is a **backtracking** engine. At every choice
(how many characters should `\w+` take? one more loop or stop?) it picks one option and remembers the others. When
the pattern fails further on, it goes back to the last choice and tries the next option.
That is fine when there are few choices. Now look at `^(\w+\s?)*$` on `aaaaaaaa!`. Each `a` can either extend the
current `\w+` or start a new loop iteration (`\s?` matches nothing). With 8 letters that is 2^7 = 128 ways to split
them, and **every** split fails at the `!`, so the engine tries them all before answering "no match".
Add one letter and the work doubles. 30 letters: about 500 million splits. That is **catastrophic backtracking**.
Two things to notice in the step debugger below:
- A matching input is fast: the first split that works wins. The explosion happens on input that **almost** matches.
- The pattern is short and looks harmless. Vulnerable patterns ship to production because they pass every normal test.

steps.prompt: Which input makes `^(\w+\s?)*$` take the longest?
options: `the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog` (it matches)
steps.explain: The sentence matches on the first try. The `!` line fails at once: no `\w` can start, so there is nothing to split. Thirty letters followed by something that breaks the match at the end is the worst case: every way of splitting the letters is tried.

steps.prompt: Can this pattern explode on input that almost matches?
buckets: Can explode: several ways to match the same text inside a repeat
Safe: each character can be matched one way
steps.explain: The warning sign is a quantifier inside a quantified group where the inner part can match a variable amount: `(a+)+`, `(\d+)*`, `(\w+\s?)*`. In `^\w+( \w+)*$` every repeat must start with a space, so there is only one way to split the words. Overlapping alternatives such as `(\w|\d)+` are the same trap: a digit can be taken by either branch.

steps.title: Fix 1: one way per character
body: The best fix is a rewrite where each character can be matched in only one way. Ask of every character: *which parts
of the pattern could take it?* If the answer is "more than one, inside a repeat", rewrite.
| Vulnerable | Rewrite | Why it is safe |
| `(a+)+` | `a+` | the outer loop added nothing but ways to split |
| `(\w\|\d)+` | `\w+` | `\d` is already inside `\w` |
| `^(\w+\s?)*$` | `^\w+( \w+)*$` | each new word must start after a space |
| `^([a-z0-9]+\.?)+@` | `^[a-z0-9]+(\.[a-z0-9]+)*@` | a dot is required between runs |
| `.*=.*` | `[^=]*=.*` | the text before the `=` cannot contain one |
Then **test the failure case**: a long run of the repeated character followed by something that breaks the match,
like 5,000 `a` and a `!`. A safe pattern answers instantly; a vulnerable one never does.

steps.title: Rewrite the word-list validator
prompt: A form field accepts a line of words separated by single spaces: no leading, trailing or double spaces. The current
pattern is `^(\w+\s?)*$`, and it hangs on 5,000 letters followed by `!`.
Write a pattern with the same purpose that answers fast. The checks match the whole text, so you do not need `^`
hints: Start with one word, then repeat "a space and a word". Every repeat now begins with a character `\w` cannot take.
steps.explain: `\w+( \w+)*` gives each character one place: letters belong to the current word, and a space always starts the next repeat. On `aaaa...!` the engine takes the letters once, fails at `!`, and has nothing else to try.

steps.title: Rewrite the email local-part check
prompt: An older signup check uses `([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@[a-zA-Z0-9]+(\.[a-zA-Z0-9]+)+`. A security scan flagged it.
Rewrite it with the same intent: before the `@`, runs of letters and digits separated by **single** dots (no dot
at the start or end, no `..`); after it, the same for the domain, with at least one dot.
hints: The domain half is already safe: every repeat starts with `\.`. Give the local part the same shape.
steps.explain: Making the dot required inside the repeat removes the ambiguity: `aaaa` can no longer be split into `a` + `aaa` + `...` iterations. The scan that flagged it was probably CodeQL's ReDoS query; you meet it in the next lesson.

steps.title: Fix 2: atomic groups
body: Sometimes a rewrite is awkward. An **atomic group** `(?>...)` matches its content once and then throws away the
remembered alternatives inside it. If the rest of the pattern fails, the engine does not come back to re-split it.
```csharp
// Same meaning as ^(\w+\s?)*$ for whole-line validation, but each iteration is final:
var words = new Regex(@"^(?>\w+\s?)*$", RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
Atomic groups change meaning when the content needs to give characters back: `(?>a+)a` can never match, because
`a+` keeps every `a`. Use them where giving back could never help, as here.
**Possessive quantifiers** (`a++`, `\w*+`) are shorthand for an atomic group around one quantifier. PCRE, Java and
Python 3.11+ have them. **.NET and JavaScript do not**: in .NET write `(?>a+)`; JavaScript has neither, so rewrite.
The .NET engine already makes some single loops atomic on its own (for example `\d+` followed by a letter), but it
cannot do that for nested or overlapping loops. Do not rely on it.

steps.prompt: Where can you write the possessive quantifier `\w++`? Select all that apply.
steps.explain: Python added atomic groups and possessive quantifiers to `re` in 3.11. .NET has atomic groups `(?>...)` but no possessive syntax. JavaScript has neither, so the fix there is a rewrite.

steps.title: Make it safe with an atomic group
prompt: A legacy validator must keep its exact behaviour: `^(\w+\s?)*$`, which also accepts the empty string and a single
whitespace character after each word (`a b\tc` and `hello world ` pass).
Keep that meaning but make it safe by putting the inside of the loop in an **atomic group**.
hints: Wrap `\w+\s?` in `(?>` and `)`, and keep the `*` outside.
steps.explain: Inside `(?>\w+\s?)` the `\w+` takes the whole run of letters and never gives any back, so there is exactly one way to split the input into iterations. The behaviour on valid input is unchanged.

steps.title: A tag list pattern that cannot hang
prompt: Blog posts carry tags like `dotnet,regex,perf`: one or more tags of lower-case ASCII letters and digits, separated
by single commas. No empty tags, no spaces, no leading or trailing comma.
Write `string TagListPattern()` that returns the pattern. The tests build it with
`new Regex(TagListPattern(), RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100))` and call `IsMatch`, so anchor it
with `^` and `$`. They also send 3,000 letters followed by `!`: a pattern like `^([a-z0-9]+,?)+$` times out there.
template: var dojoRx = new Regex(TagListPattern(), RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
Dojo.Eq("an empty tag is refused", false, dojoRx.IsMatch("dotnet,,regex"));
Dojo.Eq("a leading comma is refused", false, dojoRx.IsMatch(",dotnet"));
Dojo.Eq("a trailing comma is refused", false, dojoRx.IsMatch("dotnet,"));
Dojo.Eq("a space is refused", false, dojoRx.IsMatch("dotnet, regex"));
Dojo.Eq("the empty string is refused", false, dojoRx.IsMatch(""));
Dojo.Try("3,000 letters and ! (timed out)", () => Dojo.Eq("3,000 letters and ! is refused fast", false, dojoRx.IsMatch(new string('a', 3000) + "!")));
Dojo.Try("1,500 tags and ! (timed out)", () => Dojo.Eq("1,500 tags and ! is refused fast", false, dojoRx.IsMatch(string.Concat(Enumerable.Repeat("a,", 1500)) + "!")));
hints: One tag, then repeat "a comma and a tag": every repeat starts with a comma, so there is one way to split.
